title: Korean Mortgage Rates Hit 4.66% in August 2026
html:
At a glance
1
New bank mortgage rates rose to 4.66% in August 2026, up 0.18 percentage points from July.
2
Mortgage borrowing costs are up 0.70 percentage points compared to August 2025 and 1.15 percentage points above August 2024.
3
The 4.66% mark is the highest new bank mortgage rate recorded across the 3-year data series.

Data as of 2026-08 · Last updated 2026-10-11 · 5 min read

In this post

  1. The shift across two years of borrowing data
  2. How bank mortgage rates moved over the past year
  3. Housing market reports alongside rising rates
  4. Pressures on renters and deposit loans
  5. Primary data resources

Official lending figures from the Bank of Korea show new home loan borrowing costs reached their highest point in three years this summer, with the average rate on newly extended bank mortgage loans rising to 4.66% in August 2026 [1].

That represents a jump of 0.18 percentage points from July's 4.48%, and it leaves newly issued bank mortgage debt up 0.70 percentage points compared to the 3.96% recorded twelve months earlier [1].

For anyone examining the Korean housing market from abroad, or expats weighing whether to purchase or renew a residential lease, reading these primary numbers directly from the original Korean releases matters. Media accounts often bundle commercial bank lending rates together with targeted policy loan schemes or focus purely on asking prices. Looking straight at the central bank's newly extended credit data gives the unvarnished borrowing cost faced by market participants who take out standard bank financing.

The shift across two years of borrowing data

Two summers ago, newly extended bank mortgages sat at their lowest point in this statistical run, touching 3.50% in July 2024 and 3.51% in August 2024 [1].

Over a 24-month horizon, new bank borrowing costs have climbed 1.15 percentage points [1]. If someone had projected debt service during the quieter borrowing periods of late 2024, that 4.66% print meaningfully shifts monthly cash outflows on any substantial apartment loan in the capital.

The path upward since that low was not a straight line. Borrowing costs climbed past 4.05% in October 2024 and 4.30% in November 2024 before softening to 3.87% in May 2025 [1]. That reprieve did not hold. From late summer 2025, borrowing costs began a grinding climb that broke out sharply into the summer of 2026.

After sitting flat at 4.32% between February and May 2026, the cost of credit surged in the middle of the year, stepping up to 4.36% in June, 4.48% in July, and accelerating to 4.66% in August [1]. The entire summer move happened quickly, leaving borrowers with noticeably steeper financing terms than were available in the spring.

Housing market reports alongside rising rates

Higher interest costs have arrived while broader Seoul property reporting points to sustained price momentum. English coverage by UPI noted that Seoul apartment prices logged an 87-week run of uninterrupted gains, an observation shared in English reporting from The Chosun Ilbo [2].

Yet underneath that long streak, local geographic patterns have become uneven. Korean coverage from Energy Economy News and Korea Report indicated that while price gains broadened across the wider capital, southern prime districts like Gangnam saw softening while northern areas sustained price growth [3]. Yonhap Infomax referenced KB Real Estate figures suggesting a slower pace of price growth overall alongside declines in Gangnam [4]. Further reporting in Kyunghyang Shinmun indicated that price increases were pulled higher outside Gangnam.

I find this divergence between rising mortgage costs and stubbornly resilient prices outside the prime hubs particularly telling, as it suggests non-speculative buyers are being pushed to finance purchases at top-tier rates rather than waiting for an easing cycle that has yet to arrive.

Pressures on renters and deposit loans

For tenants weighing whether to buy or renew an existing lease, deposit dynamics introduce another layer of financial friction. Because the jeonse system requires a sizable upfront deposit often funded via bank credit, high commercial lending benchmarks feed directly into the carrying cost of holding a lease.

Korean reporting in Cheonji Ilbo pointed out that jeonse price increases actually overtook purchase price gains during that same 87-week stretch [5]. When lease deposits climb faster than sale values in an environment where bank mortgage rates touch 4.66%, tenants do not necessarily find refuge by staying in the rental pool; their borrowing requirements simply shift from a purchase mortgage to a deposit loan.

Public assistance addresses part of this gap for targeted groups. BigGo Finance reported that eligibility under the youth jeonse guarantee program expanded to age 39, with limits raised to 300 million won for newlywed and child-rearing households [6]. Anyone outside those designated policy brackets faces the unbuffered terms set by commercial lenders.

Official data and rules

  • Korea Real Estate Board R-ONE
  • Bank of Korea (English)

Questions people ask

What is the current Korean mortgage rate for new bank loans?

Official Bank of Korea ECOS statistics show new bank mortgage loans averaged 4.66% in August 2026. This is up from 4.48% in July 2026 and 4.32% in May 2026.

How much have Korean mortgage rates increased over the past year?

Over the 12 months ending in August 2026, new bank mortgage rates increased by 0.70 percentage points, rising from 3.96% in August 2025 to 4.66% in August 2026.

Primary data resources

Checking primary statistical releases remains the clearest way to evaluate these market shifts. For transaction volumes, national price measures, and property indices, see the Korea Real Estate Board R-ONE portal [7]. To consult monthly bank loan rates, credit aggregates, and underlying economic tables in English, refer directly to the Bank of Korea [8].

desc: Bank of Korea ECOS data shows new bank mortgage rates rose to 4.66% in August 2026, marking a 3-year high as housing price gains continue.
